questions.question: What is a bean definition in Spring?
questions.title: Spring Bean Definition Explained
questions.direct_answer: A Spring bean definition is metadata that tells the container how to create and manage an object. It can describe the bean class or factory method, scope, constructor arguments, property values, qualifiers, lazy behavior, and lifecycle methods. The BeanFactory stores definitions; the actual bean instance may be created later according to its scope and lazy settings.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Spring separates bean metadata (definition) from the actual object instance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking bean definition and bean instance are the same thing, when definition is the recipe and instance is the cooked meal
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Spring reads annotations or XML to create BeanDefinition objects before any beans are instantiated, showing you understand the two-phase process

sections.title: A Bean Definition Is Metadata, Not the Bean
sections.content:
Suppose @Service marks OrderService. Component scanning registers metadata for OrderService first; it does not immediately mean that the final proxied OrderService object already exists. BeanFactoryPostProcessor implementations can change definitions, then Spring resolves dependencies and creates the instance. BeanPostProcessor implementations can act before and after initialization and may return a proxy.

This is why getBeanDefinition describes configuration, while getBean returns an object. The definition contains enough information to create the object, but the instance's actual creation time depends on scope, lazy initialization, dependencies, and context behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Bean definition = creation and lifecycle metadata.
Bean = the object produced from that metadata.
Definitions can come from component scanning, @Bean methods, imports, XML, or registrars.
Singleton definitions usually produce one instance per container; lazy and prototype rules change creation time.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Spring separates the recipe from the object. Component scanning and @Bean methods register bean definitions. During context refresh or later lookup, the BeanFactory uses those definitions to choose a constructor or factory method, resolve dependencies, apply post-processors, and create an instance. A singleton definition normally leads to one shared instance in that container, while a prototype definition can produce multiple objects. This distinction explains how Spring can inspect, modify, or replace definitions before any application bean exists.

sections.title: Bean Definition at a Glance
sections.content:

blue|How You Declare It|~Three ways|@Component plus scan|@Bean in @Configuration|XML (legacy)
emerald|What Is Inside|~The recipe details|Class name and scope|Constructor args|Init/destroy callbacks
violet|Who Reads It|~The IoC container|Reads definitions first|Then instantiates beans|Lazy or eager

sections.title: Registering and Inspecting Bean Definitions
Manual new — Spring has no bean definition
Injected — Spring owns the definition
When Bean Definitions Matter in Real Projects
sections.content: You directly interact with bean definitions when **customizing Spring's behavior**. In a multi-tenant application, you might programmatically register bean definitions at runtime using **BeanDefinitionRegistry** to create tenant-specific repositories. When building a plugin system, you read JAR files and register their beans dynamically. During **testing**, you use **@TestConfiguration** to override production bean definitions with mocks. Framework developers use **BeanFactoryPostProcessor** to modify definitions before any beans are created—for example, reading encrypted properties and injecting them into bean definitions. Most freshers won't write this code daily, but understanding the definition-versus-instance split helps debug why Spring can't find a bean or why a singleton isn't behaving as expected.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing definition with instance**: Freshers often think getBeanDefinition and getBean return the same thing. The definition is metadata; the instance is the living object. Modifying a definition after startup doesn't change existing singletons.
- **Expecting definitions to exist for manual new calls**: If you write new OrderService(gateway) instead of injecting it, Spring has no bean definition for that instance—it won't be managed, proxied, or eligible for @Transactional.
- **Not realizing definitions are created at startup**: All definitions are registered during application context refresh, before any bean is instantiated. If a class isn't scanned (wrong package) or lacks @Component, no definition exists and you'll get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException at runtime.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring reads your class like a blueprint before it ever builds the object. That blueprint is the bean definition.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app where @Service UserService becomes one bean definition
speakable_v2.familiarity_override_reason: Topic resolves to spring-bean-lifecycle, so the lifecycle timeline example does not fit this bean-definition question.

beats.text: A bean definition is the metadata Spring keeps to build a bean. It's the recipe, not the bean. It holds the class, the scope, the constructor args and the lifecycle hooks. Those hooks are why @PostConstruct runs after dependency injection. Spring reads every definition at startup before it makes a single instance.

Splitting the blueprint from the object lets Spring manage scope. One definition makes one singleton, or many prototype instances, with no change to your code. It also lets Spring spot the wiring order before it builds anything.

items: Class: which type Spring should build. It's the heart of the definition.
Scope: singleton means one shared instance, prototype means a fresh one each time.
Constructor args and properties: the wiring Spring injects while building.
Lazy flag: build eagerly at startup, or wait until first use.

beats.text: @Service on UserService makes Spring register one definition: class UserService, scope singleton, one constructor arg of UserRepository. Spring then builds a single UserService and shares it everywhere. Here's the non-obvious part. There's always one definition per bean, but a prototype scope can spin many instances from that one recipe.

items: Don't mix up the definition with the instance. Counting definitions isn't the same as counting live objects.
Definitions freeze after the context refreshes. A normal Spring Boot app won't add new ones at runtime.

speakable_v2.cap: So the bean definition is Spring's recipe card. One recipe, but the number of dishes depends on the scope.

questions.question: What is the @Bean annotation and when do you use it?
questions.title: @Bean Annotation in Spring — Usage and Purpose
questions.direct_answer: @Bean marks a factory method whose returned object is registered and managed by Spring. It is commonly declared in a @Configuration class, but @Bean methods can also appear in other component classes in lite mode. Use it for third-party objects, customized construction, or explicit named/qualified instances—not only when @Component is impossible.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of how to register beans when you don't control the source code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming every @Bean method has full @Configuration proxy semantics; @Bean can also be declared in lite configuration such as a @Component, where direct inter-method calls are ordinary Java calls
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give real-world examples: registering Jackson's ObjectMapper, Spring's RestTemplate, or a DataSource from HikariCP

sections.title: Defining a Bean with @Bean
Quick revision
content: The method name is the default bean name; name/alias attributes can change it.
Method parameters are dependencies resolved by the container.
Scope, lazy behavior, initialization, and destruction can be configured.
Full @Configuration proxying affects direct calls between @Bean methods.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A configuration method can accept PaymentProperties and return an HttpClient configured with its timeout. Spring registers that returned client, injects it elsewhere, and manages lifecycle callbacks when applicable. The method can also create two clients with different names or qualifiers. This is more explicit than component scanning and works for classes from libraries that cannot carry Spring annotations.

sections.title: @Bean at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Registers a bean|Method return is the bean|Method name is the bean name|Lives in @Configuration
blue|When to Use It|~Programmatic control|Third-party classes|Conditional creation|Custom wiring
emerald|vs @Component|~Two registration styles|@Bean is explicit, a method|@Component scans a class|@Bean when you cannot edit the class
violet|Lifecycle Hooks|~Optional callbacks|initMethod / destroyMethod|Singleton by default|Called by the container

sections.title: Registering Third-Party Beans with @Bean
@Bean on a @Service method — silently ignored
@Bean inside @Configuration — registered
When to Use @Bean vs @Component
sections.content:
Use **@Bean** when you don't control the class source code. You can't add @Service to ObjectMapper or RestTemplate—they're in external JARs. Write a @Bean method to instantiate and configure them. Also use @Bean when bean creation requires **complex logic**: reading environment variables, conditional instantiation based on profiles, or multi-step configuration. For example, creating a DataSource requires setting JDBC URL, username, password, and pool size—easier to do in a method than via annotations.

Use **@Component** (or @Service, @Repository) when you own the class and it has simple construction. Most of your business logic classes—OrderService, CustomerRepository—should use @Component. If you find yourself writing trivial @Bean methods that just return new MyService(), switch to @Component on the class itself. The rule: @Component for your code, @Bean for third-party or complex setup.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Putting @Bean outside @Configuration**: Freshers annotate a regular @Service class method with @Bean. Spring ignores it unless the class is @Configuration. The method won't be called and no bean is registered.
- **Calling @Bean methods directly**: Calling objectMapper() from another method in the same class. In a @Configuration class, Spring intercepts these calls and returns the singleton. But freshers sometimes manually call the method thinking they're creating a new instance, leading to confusion about singleton behavior.
- **Not returning the object**: Writing a @Bean method that returns void or null. Spring stores null as the bean instance, causing NullPointerException when injected. Always return the configured object.
- **Forgetting method parameters inject dependencies**: Writing complex constructor logic inside the method instead of accepting dependencies as parameters. Spring can inject beans into @Bean method parameters automatically.

speakable_v2.hook: Can't put @Component on a class you don't own? @Bean is how you hand that object to Spring yourself.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app registering Jackson's ObjectMapper via a @Bean method
speakable_v2.familiarity_override_reason: Topic resolves to spring-bean-lifecycle, so the lifecycle timeline example does not fit this bean-definition question.

beats.text: @Bean is a method-level marker you put inside a @Configuration class. The method builds an object and returns it, and Spring keeps that return value as a bean. After that Spring owns it, so @PostConstruct runs after dependency injection, just like any bean.

@Component only works when you own the class and can add the marker. Third-party types like Jackson's ObjectMapper or a RestTemplate don't have it. @Bean lets you build the object in your own code and hand the result to Spring.

items: Plain form: @Bean on a no-arg method. Spring calls it once and keeps the return value.
Named: @Bean(name="reportMapper") replaces the default method-name bean name.
With parameters: Spring injects each one from the context, then calls your method.
Mix in @Scope, @Primary, or @Lazy when you want more control.

beats.text: Say you want Jackson's ObjectMapper as a bean. You don't own Jackson's code. So you write an objectMapper() method in your config class and return a ready instance. Here's the non-obvious part. Put that method in a plain @Component instead of @Configuration and Spring skips the proxy, so two calls build two objects.

items: @Bean only fires inside a @Configuration class. Drop it on a @Service method and Spring ignores it.
Return the object, never void. A void @Bean method hands Spring nothing to register.

speakable_v2.cap: So @Bean is your escape hatch for classes you cannot annotate. Write the method, return the object, and Spring runs the rest.

questions.question: What is @Configuration in Spring and how is it different from @Component?
questions.title: @Configuration vs @Component in Spring
questions.direct_answer: @Configuration is a specialized @Component used as a source of @Bean definitions. With proxyBeanMethods=true, its @Bean method calls can be intercepted so one bean method calling another receives the container-managed instance. An ordinary @Component can also declare @Bean methods in lite mode, but direct Java calls between those methods are not intercepted. Set proxyBeanMethods=false when inter-bean method calls are not needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding full @Configuration method interception and how it differs from lite @Bean methods; the container, not CGLIB alone, owns bean scope
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming direct @Bean method calls behave the same in full and lite configuration; proxyBeanMethods=false uses ordinary Java calls while container lookups still honor scope
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what happens if you call a @Bean method directly from another @Bean method in a @Configuration class versus a plain @Component class

sections.title: @Configuration and Ordinary Component Classes
Quick revision
content: Both annotations register the class as a Spring component.
@Configuration is intended to group @Bean factory methods.
Full configuration mode can proxy inter-bean method calls.
Lite mode and proxyBeanMethods=false use normal Java calls; inject method parameters instead of calling another factory method.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @Component registers the class itself as a bean. @Configuration also registers the class, but signals that it contains bean definitions. Its default full mode uses a generated subclass to intercept calls between @Bean methods, preserving container semantics such as a singleton reference. That statement needs a boundary: @Bean methods on ordinary components are lite configuration, and @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false) also disables interception. Modern configuration often avoids direct factory-method calls and asks Spring to inject dependencies as @Bean method parameters, allowing proxyBeanMethods=false.

sections.title: @Configuration vs @Component
sections.content:
amber|@Configuration|~Defines @Bean methods|CGLIB-proxied class|Inter-bean calls return the singleton|The factory of beans
blue|@Component|~A scanned bean itself|No @Bean proxying|Just registers this class|A regular component
emerald|The Key Trap|~Inter-bean method calls|@Configuration caches the singleton|@Component makes a new object each call|The proxy is the difference
violet|When to Use|~Pick by intent|@Configuration for @Bean factories|@Component for services/utilities|Do not mix roles

sections.title: @Configuration vs @Component
sections.content:
| Aspect | @Configuration | @Component |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary purpose | Bean definition factory class | Register class itself as bean |
| CGLIB proxy | Yes, intercepts @Bean method calls | No proxy, direct instantiation |
| @Bean methods | Fully supported, singleton enforced | Ignored by Spring container |
| Inter-bean calls | Returns cached singleton | Calls method directly, new instance |
| Typical use case | Third-party bean registration | Business logic beans (services, repos) |

sections.title: @Component with @Bean methods - duplicates
@Configuration keeps singletons
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **@Configuration** when your class contains **@Bean** methods to register other beans—especially third-party classes or beans needing complex setup. For example, an AppConfig class that creates ObjectMapper, DataSource, and RestTemplate beans. The CGLIB proxy ensures that if one @Bean method calls another @Bean method, you get the singleton, not a new instance.

Use **@Component** (or @Service, @Repository, @Controller) when the class itself is the bean. Your OrderService, CustomerRepository, PaymentController—these are business logic components. They don't produce other beans; they are the beans. If you accidentally use @Component on a class with @Bean methods, those methods are plain Java methods—Spring doesn't call them or register their return values. If one @Bean method calls another in a @Component class, you'll get multiple instances instead of singletons, causing subtle bugs like transaction managers being different across DAOs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @Component for config classes**: Freshers write a config class with @Bean methods but annotate it with @Component instead of @Configuration. The @Bean methods aren't recognized, and no beans are registered. Even if Spring somehow processes them, calling one @Bean method from another creates a new instance every time instead of returning the singleton.
- **Not understanding the proxy**: Freshers call a @Bean method directly in a @Configuration class and wonder why their initialization logic runs once but they expected multiple times. The CGLIB proxy caches the result. If you want a new instance on every call, use prototype scope, not repeated method calls.
- **Overusing @Configuration**: Making every class @Configuration when it should be @Service. @Configuration is for factory classes, not business logic. Your OrderService shouldn't be @Configuration—it should be @Service.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 AppConfig where one @Bean method calls another
speakable_v2.familiarity_override_reason: This compares @Configuration with @Component, so the auto-config starter example does not fit.

values: Build a new object each call.

beats.text: Reach for @Configuration whenever you define @Bean methods, since the proxy keeps singletons correct. Turn on @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false) when those methods never call each other, for a faster start. Use @Component for plain services, listeners, and utilities.
In an AppConfig, beanA() calls beanC() directly. With @Configuration, the proxy returns the same C that beanB() already got. Important: switch to @Component and A and B each get a different C.

questions.question: What is @Lazy in Spring and when would you use it?
questions.title: @Lazy Bean Initialization in Spring
questions.direct_answer: @Lazy on a bean definition requests deferred initialization until the bean is needed. @Lazy on an injection point can inject a lazy-resolution proxy. Non-lazy singleton beans are normally pre-instantiated when an ApplicationContext refreshes, while prototypes and other scopes already follow their own creation rules. @Lazy can break one construction-time cycle, but that often hides a design problem and moves failures to first use.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring's eager versus lazy initialization strategies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overusing @Lazy to speed up startup without understanding it hides errors that eager initialization would catch
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the trade-off: @Lazy improves startup time but moves initialization errors from startup to runtime when the bean is first used

sections.title: What @Lazy Defers
sections.content:
Lazy does not mean a new instance per access; scope still decides instance count. A lazy singleton is created once on first resolution and then reused. A prototype requested through a provider can be created repeatedly.

Initialization can still happen earlier when another non-lazy bean depends on the lazy definition directly without a lazy proxy. Test both startup and first-use behavior and ensure concurrent first access is safe through the container.

**Example.** If ReportGenerator is marked @Lazy and no request ever asks for it, Spring may finish startup without constructing it. The first bean lookup or injection through a lazy proxy triggers construction, so a broken configuration can fail at first use instead of startup.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Definition-level @Lazy delays creation of that singleton.
Injection-point @Lazy supplies a proxy that resolves the target later.
Global lazy initialization can be enabled in Boot but delays startup validation broadly.
Use it for real deferred cost or optional infrastructure, not as the default circular-dependency repair.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A rarely used report client with expensive startup can be a reasonable lazy bean. The first call then pays creation cost and may reveal missing configuration, so latency and failure timing change. Putting @Lazy on one constructor parameter can allow two beans to be constructed through a proxy, but the runtime dependency cycle remains. Splitting responsibilities or introducing an event/callback boundary is usually clearer.

For example, a rarely used ReportGenerator can be lazy so it is created only on first use. The trade-off is that its initialization delay or configuration error also moves to that first request.

sections.title: @Lazy at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|What It Does|~Delays bean creation|Not created at startup|Built on first use|Opposite of eager
blue|Default Behavior|~Singletons are eager|All built at boot|@Lazy flips this|Per-bean or per-config
emerald|When to Use|~Costly or rarely used|Heavy init beans|Can break some cycles|Faster startup
rose|Watch Out|~Hides errors|Config bugs surface late|Loses fail-fast safety|Use sparingly

sections.title: Step 1: Decide If Startup Time Is the Bottleneck
sections.content: First, measure your actual startup time and profile where it's spent. If your Spring Boot app starts in under 5 seconds, lazy initialization won't make a noticeable difference. If it's taking 30+ seconds because you have heavyweight beans—DataSource with connection pool preloading, Elasticsearch client with cluster health checks, large machine learning model loading—then @Lazy can help. Use @Lazy on those specific expensive beans, not everywhere. The key question: is the slow bean essential for the first request? If your app can't serve any request without the database, lazy-loading the DataSource just shifts the delay from startup to the first HTTP request. If the ML model is only needed for a specific admin feature, @Lazy makes sense—don't block startup for a feature 1% of requests use.

sections.title: Step 2: Understand the Error Detection Trade-off
sections.content: Eager initialization catches errors early—at startup, in your face, before production traffic hits. If you misspelled a @Value property, forgot to add a required dependency, or have a circular reference, you know immediately. @Lazy defers these errors. The app starts successfully, passes health checks, and deploys. Then the first user request tries to access the lazy bean, it fails to initialize, and you get a runtime exception. In cloud environments with auto-scaling, this can be catastrophic—new instances pass health checks but crash under load. Use @Lazy sparingly: only on beans where the startup cost is genuinely painful and the bean isn't used by every request. Never use @Lazy globally with spring.main.lazy-initialization=true in production unless you have comprehensive integration tests that touch every code path. That global flag hides all startup errors.

sections.title: Declaring and Injecting a @Lazy Bean
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Lazy everywhere to fix slow startup**: Freshers see a 15-second startup and annotate every bean with @Lazy. This masks the real problem (inefficient initialization logic) and moves errors to runtime. Fix the root cause instead—optimize database queries in @PostConstruct, remove unnecessary eager loading, or split heavyweight beans into separate modules.
- **Not understanding proxy behavior**: When you inject a @Lazy bean, Spring injects a proxy, not the real object. The first method call on that proxy triggers bean creation. Freshers sometimes serialize or reflect on the proxy and get confused by CGLIB classes in stack traces.
- **Using @Lazy to break circular dependencies without fixing the design**: Circular dependencies indicate poor design—two beans shouldn't depend on each other. @Lazy papers over the symptom but doesn't fix the coupling. Refactor one bean to use an event or callback instead of direct dependency.

seo.metaTitle: @Lazy Bean Initialization in Spring — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is @Lazy in Spring and when would you use it? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Faster startup sounds great. But @Lazy trades that speed for hidden config errors that only surface on first use.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with a heavy @Lazy ReportEngine bean
speakable_v2.familiarity_override_reason: Topic resolves to spring-bean-lifecycle, so the lifecycle timeline example does not fit this bean-definition question.

beats.text: @Lazy tells Spring to wait and build a bean on first use instead of at startup. By default Spring builds every singleton eagerly when the app starts. With @Lazy, Spring injects a stand-in proxy first. Spring builds the real bean on the first call, and like any bean, @PostConstruct runs after dependency injection.

You'd use @Lazy to cut startup time or save resources. Some beans are heavy to build, like a big connection pool or an ML model. If only a few requests need them, building them at startup wastes time for everyone.

items: @Lazy on a @Bean or @Component: that one bean waits until first use.
@Lazy on an injection point: Spring injects a proxy, then builds the bean on the first method call.
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true: makes every bean lazy, handy in dev, risky in prod.

beats.text: Picture a ReportEngine that loads slowly and runs once a day. Mark it @Lazy and startup stays quick. The job pays the cost only when someone asks for a report. Here's the non-obvious part. A typo in that lazy bean won't show at startup, so the app boots green and fails on the first report.

items: Don't sprinkle @Lazy everywhere to mask slow startup. Profile first and fix the heavy bean instead.
Using @Lazy to dodge a circular dependency hides a design smell, not a real fix.

speakable_v2.cap: So @Lazy is a sharp tool for heavy, optional beans. Don't reach for it just to make startup look faster.

questions.question: What is bean naming in Spring and how do you set a custom bean name?
questions.title: Spring Bean Naming Conventions
questions.direct_answer: Spring assigns a default name to a scanned component from its class name using JavaBeans-style decapitalization, so UserService becomes userService while an acronym name such as URLService may remain URLService. An @Bean method uses its method name by default. @Component/@Bean name attributes set names; @Qualifier adds candidate-selection metadata and does not generally rename the bean.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of Spring's bean naming conventions and why names matter
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the default lowercase-first-letter convention or that you can have multiple beans of the same type distinguished by name
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when you'd need custom names: when you have multiple beans of the same type and use @Qualifier to select which one to inject

sections.title: Spring Bean Names, Aliases, and Qualifiers
sections.content:
Most code should inject by type and use meaningful qualifiers only when several candidates implement the same role. Direct context.getBean(name) calls couple code to the container and are rarely necessary.

Default naming edge cases make generated names a poor external contract. Use explicit names when infrastructure refers to a bean by name, and use custom qualifier annotations when the selection means something such as @Live or @Batch.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Component default names use AnnotationBeanNameGenerator/decapitalization rules.
@Bean default name is the factory method name.
Explicit names and aliases are available on @Component and @Bean.
Qualifiers narrow autowiring candidates; they are not simply bean-name setters.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
@Service("billingService") assigns an explicit component name. @Bean({"paymentClient", "primaryPaymentClient"}) can give one object a main name and alias. @Qualifier("live") on a bean and injection point selects a semantic candidate even when the bean has another name. A string qualifier can also fall back against a bean name, which is why the two concepts are related but not identical.

For example, @Component on PaymentService normally registers paymentService, while @Component("cardPaymentService") gives it an explicit name that can be referenced by @Qualifier("cardPaymentService").

sections.title: Bean Naming at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Default Name|~If you set none|Class name, lower first letter|OrderService to orderService|@Bean uses method name
blue|Custom Names|~Override the default|@Component("myName")|@Bean("myName")|Or @Qualifier
emerald|Why Names Matter|~Disambiguation|Pick among many beans|Qualifier by name|XML / SpEL references
violet|Aliases|~Multiple names|@Bean(name={"a","b"})|All point to one bean|Handy for migration

sections.title: Setting Custom Bean Names
When Custom Bean Names Matter
sections.content: Use **custom bean names** when you have multiple beans of the same type and need to distinguish them. Scenario 1: **Multiple data sources**—you might have "primaryDatabase" and "analyticsDatabase" beans, both of type DataSource, and services inject the one they need using @Qualifier. Scenario 2: **Different configurations of the same tool**—like "fastRestTemplate" with 2-second timeout and "slowRestTemplate" with 30-second timeout for external APIs. Scenario 3: **Descriptive names for clarity**—naming a bean "paymentProcessor" instead of letting it default to "stripePaymentServiceImpl" makes configuration more readable. The rule: if someone reading your @Qualifier annotation needs to understand what makes this bean special, give it a clear custom name.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing the lowercase convention**: Freshers often look for a bean named "UserService" when Spring registered it as "userService"—the default name lowercases the first letter.
- **Forgetting that @Bean uses method name**: If your method is named `customerRepo()` but returns a CustomerRepository, the bean name is "customerRepo" not "customerRepository"—you must use that exact name in @Qualifier.
- **Using custom names everywhere**: Don't customize names unless you need to—if you only have one UserService bean, the default name works fine and changing it just adds confusion. Only customize when you have multiple beans of the same type or when the default name isn't clear enough.

How do you look up a bean by name programmatically?

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is bean naming in Spring and how do you set a custom bean name? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring names your beans for free. But with two beans of one type, that name is how you pick the right one.
speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with two DataSource beans picked apart by @Qualifier
speakable_v2.familiarity_override_reason: Topic resolves to spring-bean-lifecycle, so the lifecycle timeline example does not fit this bean-definition question.

beats.text: A bean name is just a string id Spring uses to store and look up a bean. @Component types default to the class name with a lowercase first letter, and @Bean methods use the method name. The name sticks through the bean's life, so @PostConstruct runs after dependency injection on the bean you looked up.
Names solve ambiguity. With two beans of the same type, matching by type alone fails. @Qualifier uses the name to pick one. The same name also drives applicationContext.getBean() lookups.

items: @Service or @Component: the class name with a lowercase first letter, so UserService becomes userService.
@Bean method: the method name, so primaryDataSource() registers a bean named primaryDataSource.
Custom name: @Component("myBean") or @Bean(name="myBean") overrides the default.
Aliases: @Bean(name={"primaryDs", "mainDs"}) answers to either name.

beats.text: Picture two DataSource beans, devDataSource() and prodDataSource(). Their names match the methods. You inject one with @Qualifier("devDataSource"). Here's the sharp edge. Rename the method to devDb and the bean name changes too, so every @Qualifier("devDataSource") quietly breaks.

items: Rename a @Bean method and the default bean name changes with it, breaking existing @Qualifier references.
Two beans can't share one name in a context. Spring throws BeanDefinitionOverrideException unless you allow overriding.

speakable_v2.cap: So learn the default rule, name beans you'll reference with @Qualifier, and don't let a rename silently change a name you depend on.
